source_text: Return to the eighty-kilobase example, open Bodies and add Whole nucleus. The modeled region still sits inside its own confinement sphere, while a much larger soft envelope represents the nuclear periphery. The region is a small part of the nucleus, so one side of it meets the envelope. By default that is the side away from the nucleolus, which faces the nuclear interior; you can move the envelope. Then add tethering elements: genomic intervals, such as lamina-associated domains, whose beads can attach to the envelope or to a landmark surface. Each bead within the capture distance attaches with its own hazard and, once attached, feels a spring to a fixed anchor. Attachment can require a mark and an occupied nucleosome, and vacant sites can release faster. In 3D, tick Whole nucleus to frame the envelope, and look for amber tether links. In 1D genome, the Tethers row shows attached beads, and the Nucleosomes row marks every vacant site. Tethers are phenomenological anchors, not lamina proteins.
